screens.title: Functions and Modular Programming
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn how to take repeated or complex behavior and encapsulate it into named, reusable pieces called functions. Functions let you give a clear role to each part of a sketch: one block reads sensors, another updates displays, another controls actuators. This reduces repetition and makes debugging far easier because each block has one responsibility. We'll practice writing functions with parameters that accept inputs, returning values when a computation is needed, and writing void routines that perform actions without returning data. You'll also see how variable scope affects where data lives, why global variables should be limited, and when to pass values in and out. As a practical thread through the lesson, we'll use a kitchen analogy: functions are cooks who receive ingredients, follow a recipe, and deliver a dish. By the end you'll be able to refactor a long loop into distinct functions like readSensor, printValue, and blinkLED, and explain why that improves clarity and testability. Think about a function you might write for your own project—what single responsibility could it take on?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Functions package behavior into named blocks to improve reuse, readability, and testing.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Functions & Modular Programming
Functions and Modular Programming
Design reusable code blocks that accept inputs, perform a task, and optionally return results.
Why this matters: small, focused functions make sketches easier to read, easier to test, and safer to change. When each function has one responsibility, you can reason locally and reduce bugs that span the whole program.
In this lesson
Define functions
Learn parameter, return type, and scope basics with examples.
Coming up
Refactor a loop
Split a long loop into read, print, and blink functions for clarity.
Hands-on
Kitchen analogy
Each function is a cook receiving ingredients and returning a dish.
Kitchen analogy
Cook receives ingredients (parameters), follows a recipe (body), delivers a dish (return).
Example preview
int add(int a, int b) {
  return a + b;
}

void blinkLED(int pin, int duration) {
  digitalWrite(pin, HIGH);
  delay(duration);
  digitalWrite(pin, LOW);
  delay(duration);
}
Key Takeaway

Start small: give each function a single job and prefer parameters over globals to keep behavior predictable.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practice and assessment. First, you will be able to define and call your own functions on Arduino: write declarations, choose names, set parameter types, and invoke the function correctly from setup or loop. Second, you will understand parameters, return values, and variable scope: what data is local to a function, what is global, and when to return values versus updating shared state. Third, you'll learn to organize code into reusable blocks so you can split a long sketch into focused routines, which makes it easier to test and change without breaking unrelated behavior. Finally, you'll explain the difference between local and global variables and apply that knowledge in refactoring. Each objective pairs a coding skill with a practical reason: readability, testability, and fewer bugs. Throughout the lesson we use a kitchen analogy and a step-by-step refactor activity so you can practice writing and calling functions with confidence.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Assessment
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on practice. You will refactor a long loop by extracting three functions: readSensor, printValue, and blinkLED. That exercise translates theory into habit: each function should have a single responsibility and be easy to test. You will also identify return types and parameters on short code snippets, explaining why a function returns data or uses void. For assessment, you will convert an analog reading into a voltage by writing a function that maps a zero-to-ten-twenty-three reading to a zero-to-five-point-zero voltage; this is a concrete task that checks your understanding of parameters, return values, and numeric types. Practice writing local variables inside functions and confirm they are not accessible outside. Finally, reflect on where a global variable is actually needed, such as shared hardware objects, and where it creates hidden coupling. These practice goals make the learning measurable and transfer immediately to real Arduino projects.

screens.title: What is a function?
screens.narratorSegment: A function is a named block of code that performs a specific task and can be reused anywhere in a sketch. In Arduino, functions have a return type, a name, optional parameters, and a body. The return type tells the compiler whether the function produces a value — for example, an integer or a floating decimal — or produces nothing, expressed as void. Parameters are the inputs that the function needs to do its work; they act like ingredients handed to a cook. Local variables declared inside the function exist only while that function runs and are destroyed when it ends. This scoping prevents accidental interference between unrelated parts of a program. A concrete example is an add function that takes two integers and returns their sum. That small unit encapsulates a single arithmetic responsibility and can be called wherever addition of two integers is needed. A common misconception is thinking a function must be long or complicated; in practice, the best functions are short and focused. When you write functions with one responsibility, your sketches become more modular and easier to test. How would you name a function that only reads one sensor?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Functions are small, named units of behavior with optional inputs and an optional result.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › What is a function?
Function anatomy
Return type • Name • Parameters • Body
int add(int a, int b) {
  return a + b;
}
This simple add function takes two integer ingredients and returns their sum. It demonstrates the four parts clearly and is fully reusable wherever integer addition is needed.
Local variable
Exists only during the function call.
Global variable
Declared outside functions and visible everywhere.
Analogy — kitchen cook
Think of a function as a cook who receives ingredients, follows a recipe, and returns a dish. The cook's workspace and utensils are local; other cooks do not see them unless the finished dish is shared.
Example
A conversion function that maps analog readings to voltage is a focused function: it takes a reading and returns a numeric voltage.
Key Takeaway

Keep functions focused. Short, single-purpose functions are easier to reuse and test.

screens.title: Return types and parameters
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding parameters and return types is central to using functions effectively. Parameters are the inputs you give when you call a function; they let the function operate on different data without changing its code. For example, a blink routine can accept a pin number and a duration so the same routine blinks different LEDs at different speeds. Return types tell you whether the function produces a value back to the caller. A function that computes a sum should return that value so the caller can store or use it. In Arduino, you use concrete types like int or float for returns and parameter types. A common error is to use void when you actually need a value later; that hides the result and forces the use of globals instead. Here, we'll step through a short code example that shows a conversion function for analog readings: it accepts an integer reading and returns a floating-point voltage. Then we'll contrast that with a void routine that toggles an LED without returning anything. The contrast helps clarify when to return values and when to use void.

keyIdea.title: Parameters & returns
keyIdea.text: Pass inputs for flexibility; return results when the calling code needs computed values instead of shared state.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Return types & Parameters
Code examples
A conversion function and a void action routine.
float toVoltage(int reading) {
  // map 0-1023 to 0.0-5.0
  return (reading / 1023.0) * 5.0;
}

void blinkLED(int pin, int duration) {
  digitalWrite(pin, HIGH);
  delay(duration);
  digitalWrite(pin, LOW);
  delay(duration);
}
Use when toVoltage
You need the numeric voltage for display or math; so return it.
Use when blinkLED
It performs an action on hardware and doesn't need to return a value, so void is appropriate.
Concrete example
Call toVoltage with a sensor reading, store the returned value, and print it. Call blinkLED with different durations to vary blink speed.
Common mistake
Choosing void because it's simple prevents you from returning useful computed results. If a result is needed later, return it instead of writing it to a global variable.
Key Takeaway

Decide whether a function should return a value based on whether callers need that result to proceed.

screens.title: Local vs Global Variables
screens.narratorSegment: Scope determines where a variable can be read and modified. Local variables are declared inside a function and only exist for the duration of that function call. Global variables are declared outside any function and can be accessed or changed by any function in the sketch. Locals reduce accidental interference because each function manages its own temporary data. Globals are convenient for sharing hardware references or configuration constants across functions, but overuse leads to hidden coupling and makes reasoning about state harder. A practical trade-off is to keep hardware handles global while keeping sensor readings and intermediate values local or passed as parameters. For instance, keep the pin constant global but pass the measured value into display or logic functions. A common misbelief is that using globals is simpler — it may be in the short term, but it creates brittle code as projects grow. Prefer passing inputs and returning outputs to keep functions independent and easier to test. Local vs Global Variables means prefer local variables and parameter passing; reserve globals for shared hardware objects or constants.. In practical terms, scope rules and practical trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Scope rule
keyIdea.text: Prefer local variables and parameter passing; reserve globals for shared hardware objects or constants.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Local vs Global Variables
Local variables
Declared inside functions; lifetime is the function call.
void example(){ int temp = analogRead(A0); // temp exists only here }
Local variables keep functions independent. When you test a function, you only need to supply its inputs and observe its outputs, not the whole program state.
Global variables
Declared outside functions and available everywhere in the sketch.
const int LED_PIN = 13; // hardware pin constant int sharedState = 0; // mutable global
Use globals for hardware constants or objects, but minimize mutable globals to avoid hard-to-find bugs.
Pro tip
Pass values as parameters and return results instead of relying on globals. That keeps functions portable and easier to reuse in different sketches.
Key Takeaway

Favor local scope and explicit data flow; use globals sparingly for shared hardware and constants.

screens.title: Writing a void action routine
screens.narratorSegment: Void functions are routines that perform actions but do not return a value. These are common in Arduino because many tasks are about controlling hardware: setting pin outputs, toggling relays, or updating displays. When designing a void routine, think about what inputs it needs to perform the action and nothing more. For example, a blink routine should accept a pin number and a duration. This design lets the same routine operate different LEDs or blink speeds without duplication. In practice, call the routine from loop with different arguments to reuse behavior. Avoid embedding long delays or blocking operations inside many void routines that run frequently, because that can make the sketch unresponsive. If you need non-blocking behavior, consider designing functions that perform a small step and return quickly so the main loop can orchestrate timing. A common misconception is that void means low complexity — the key is to keep responsibilities small and avoid hidden side effects. Writing a void action routine means use void for action-focused functions and keep them parameterized so the same routine can serve multiple contexts.. In practical terms, designing functions that perform hardware actions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Void routines
keyIdea.text: Use void for action-focused functions and keep them parameterized so the same routine can serve multiple contexts.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Void action routines
Design steps
1. Identify the single action the routine must perform.
2. Decide what inputs are required (parameters).
3. Avoid returning values; keep side effects explicit and limited.
4. Keep the routine short and avoid long blocking times when possible.
void blinkLED(int pin, int duration) { digitalWrite(pin, HIGH); delay(duration); digitalWrite(pin, LOW); delay(duration); }
Concrete scenario
You have two status LEDs. Call blinkLED with different pins and durations to indicate different states without duplicating code.
Common mistake: embedding global state changes deep inside many void routines. If an action changes many globals, it becomes harder to find the source of bugs.
Key Takeaway

Parameterize void routines so one implementation serves many cases and avoids duplicated code.

screens.title: Split responsibilities — single responsibility principle
screens.narratorSegment: As projects grow, a single long loop becomes hard to read and change. Following the single responsibility principle, split loop logic into small functions where each has one job. For example, break a sketch into readSensors, updateDisplay, checkAlarms, and controlMotors. Each function can be developed and tested independently. ReadSensors returns the raw measurements; updateDisplay accepts those values and handles presentation; checkAlarms evaluates thresholds and triggers alerts; controlMotors handles actuators based on computed commands. When you structure code this way, you can unit-test logic in isolation or simulate inputs without hardware. Another benefit is clearer naming: a function name conveys intent and becomes documentation. A common pitfall is over-splitting into too many tiny functions that create overhead; aim for balanced boundaries where each function is meaningful and testable. This approach also makes it easier to reuse or replace parts as a project evolves. Split responsibilities — single responsibility principle means split behavior into named functions so each part is testable and understandable on its own.. In practical terms, organize loop behavior into focused functions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Modularity
keyIdea.text: Split behavior into named functions so each part is testable and understandable on its own.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Split responsibilities
Architectural pattern
Break the main loop into meaningful functions representing steps in the program flow.
Example flow
  1. readSensors() — gather sensor values and return readings.
  2. checkAlarms() — evaluate thresholds and set flags.
  3. controlMotors() — compute and apply actuator commands.
  4. updateDisplay() — present values and statuses.
Concrete example
Instead of one monolithic loop, call these four functions in sequence from loop. Each function can be simulated or unit-tested with sample inputs to validate behavior without running the whole device.
Misconception: splitting always improves performance. Splitting improves clarity and testability; performance depends on how functions are implemented and whether they block frequently.
Key Takeaway

Group code by responsibility. That makes maintenance and evolution of your project much simpler.

screens.title: Before and after: refactoring loop()
screens.narratorSegment: Refactoring means extracting repeated or related code into functions. Consider a long loop that reads a sensor, prints the value, and blinks an LED. In the before state, all logic is inline: reading, formatting, printing, and blinking are mixed together. That makes it hard to change any part without touching others. In the after state, extract readSensor to return the raw reading, printValue to accept the reading and handle formatting and printing, and blinkLED to perform the blink action. Now the main loop simply calls these three functions in order. Each small function can be tested independently: simulate a reading and verify print formatting, test blink parameters without touching sensor code. Using this pattern also reduces duplication if you later need to read and print a different sensor: reuse the same printValue function. A common pitfall during refactor is forgetting to return or pass values so functions remain coupled through globals; prefer explicit parameters and returns when possible. Before and after: refactoring loop() means extracting focused functions from a long loop improves readability and testing while preserving behavior.. In practical terms, split a sketch into readsensor, printvalue, and blinkled. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Refactor pattern
keyIdea.text: Extracting focused functions from a long loop improves readability and testing while preserving behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Refactor: before & after
Before (inline loop)
void loop() {
  int reading = analogRead(A0);
  float v = (reading / 1023.0) * 5.0;
  Serial.println(v);
  digitalWrite(13, HIGH);
  delay(500);
  digitalWrite(13, LOW);
  delay(500);
}
All steps are mixed, which makes small changes risky.
After (refactored)
int readSensor() { return analogRead(A0); }
float toVoltage(int r) { return (r / 1023.0) * 5.0; }
void printValue(float v) { Serial.println(v); }
void blinkLED(int pin, int d) { digitalWrite(pin, HIGH); delay(d); digitalWrite(pin, LOW); delay(d); }

void loop() {
  int r = readSensor();
  float v = toVoltage(r);
  printValue(v);
  blinkLED(13, 500);
}
Each function has a single role and is easier to test and reuse.
Key Takeaway

Refactoring does not change behavior when done carefully, but it makes code easier to understand and extend. Prefer explicit parameters and return values over hidden globals.

screens.title: Refactor practice with a kitchen analogy
screens.narratorSegment: For practice, imagine a small kitchen with three cooks: a sensor reader, a printer, and a blinker. The reader cook accepts an ingredient request and returns a measurement. The printer cook accepts a numeric ingredient and formats it for delivery to the diner. The blinker cook accepts a pin and a timing ingredient and performs the blink action. When you refactor a single long loop, extract these cooks into separate functions so each has a single recipe. Write readSensor to return an integer reading; write printValue to accept a floating voltage and print it; write blinkLED to accept pin and duration and toggle hardware. Test each function independently: simulate a sensor reading to check print formatting; call blinkLED with varying durations to confirm timing. Watch for a common error: using global variables for intermediate values instead of passing them into functions. Passing and returning values makes the cooks independent and the kitchen easier to manage and debug. In practical terms, each function is a specialized cook with a clear recipe. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how to take repeated or complex behavior and encapsulate it into named, reusable pieces called functions. Functions let you give a clear role to each part of a sketch: one block reads sensors, another updates displays, another controls actuators. This reduces repetition and makes debugging far easier because each block has one responsibility. We'll practice writing functions with parameters that accept inputs, returning values when a computation is needed, and writing void routines that perform actions without returning data. You'll also see how variable scope affects where data lives, why global variables should be limited, and when to pass values in and out. As a practical thread through the lesson, we'll use a kitchen analogy: functions are cooks who receive ingredients, follow a recipe, and deliver a dish. By the end you'll be able to refactor a long loop into distinct functions like readSensor, printValue, and blinkLED, and explain why that improves clarity and testability. Think about a function you might write for your own project—what single responsibility could it take on?

These objectives map to practice and assessment. First, you will be able to define and call your own functions on Arduino: write declarations, choose names, set parameter types, and invoke the function correctly from setup or loop. Second, you will understand parameters, return values, and variable scope: what data is local to a function, what is global, and when to return values versus updating shared state. Third, you'll learn to organize code into reusable blocks so you can split a long sketch into focused routines, which makes it easier to test and change without breaking unrelated behavior. Finally, you'll explain the difference between local and global variables and apply that knowledge in refactoring. Each objective pairs a coding skill with a practical reason: readability, testability, and fewer bugs. Throughout the lesson we use a kitchen analogy and a step-by-step refactor activity so you can practice writing and calling functions with confidence.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice. You will refactor a long loop by extracting three functions: readSensor, printValue, and blinkLED. That exercise translates theory into habit: each function should have a single responsibility and be easy to test. You will also identify return types and parameters on short code snippets, explaining why a function returns data or uses void. For assessment, you will convert an analog reading into a voltage by writing a function that maps a zero-to-ten-twenty-three reading to a zero-to-five-point-zero voltage; this is a concrete task that checks your understanding of parameters, return values, and numeric types. Practice writing local variables inside functions and confirm they are not accessible outside. Finally, reflect on where a global variable is actually needed, such as shared hardware objects, and where it creates hidden coupling. These practice goals make the learning measurable and transfer immediately to real Arduino projects.

A function is a named block of code that performs a specific task and can be reused anywhere in a sketch. In Arduino, functions have a return type, a name, optional parameters, and a body. The return type tells the compiler whether the function produces a value — for example, an integer or a floating decimal — or produces nothing, expressed as void. Parameters are the inputs that the function needs to do its work; they act like ingredients handed to a cook. Local variables declared inside the function exist only while that function runs and are destroyed when it ends. This scoping prevents accidental interference between unrelated parts of a program. A concrete example is an add function that takes two integers and returns their sum. That small unit encapsulates a single arithmetic responsibility and can be called wherever addition of two integers is needed. A common misconception is thinking a function must be long or complicated; in practice, the best functions are short and focused. When you write functions with one responsibility, your sketches become more modular and easier to test. How would you name a function that only reads one sensor?

Understanding parameters and return types is central to using functions effectively. Parameters are the inputs you give when you call a function; they let the function operate on different data without changing its code. For example, a blink routine can accept a pin number and a duration so the same routine blinks different LEDs at different speeds. Return types tell you whether the function produces a value back to the caller. A function that computes a sum should return that value so the caller can store or use it. In Arduino, you use concrete types like int or float for returns and parameter types. A common error is to use void when you actually need a value later; that hides the result and forces the use of globals instead. Here, we'll step through a short code example that shows a conversion function for analog readings: it accepts an integer reading and returns a floating-point voltage. Then we'll contrast that with a void routine that toggles an LED without returning anything. The contrast helps clarify when to return values and when to use void.

Scope determines where a variable can be read and modified. Local variables are declared inside a function and only exist for the duration of that function call. Global variables are declared outside any function and can be accessed or changed by any function in the sketch. Locals reduce accidental interference because each function manages its own temporary data. Globals are convenient for sharing hardware references or configuration constants across functions, but overuse leads to hidden coupling and makes reasoning about state harder. A practical trade-off is to keep hardware handles global while keeping sensor readings and intermediate values local or passed as parameters. For instance, keep the pin constant global but pass the measured value into display or logic functions. A common misbelief is that using globals is simpler — it may be in the short term, but it creates brittle code as projects grow. Prefer passing inputs and returning outputs to keep functions independent and easier to test. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Void functions are routines that perform actions but do not return a value. These are common in Arduino because many tasks are about controlling hardware: setting pin outputs, toggling relays, or updating displays. When designing a void routine, think about what inputs it needs to perform the action and nothing more. For example, a blink routine should accept a pin number and a duration. This design lets the same routine operate different LEDs or blink speeds without duplication. In practice, call the routine from loop with different arguments to reuse behavior. Avoid embedding long delays or blocking operations inside many void routines that run frequently, because that can make the sketch unresponsive. If you need non-blocking behavior, consider designing functions that perform a small step and return quickly so the main loop can orchestrate timing. A common misconception is that void means low complexity — the key is to keep responsibilities small and avoid hidden side effects. As projects grow, a single long loop becomes hard to read and change. Following the single responsibility principle, split loop logic into small functions where each has one job. For example, break a sketch into readSensors, updateDisplay, checkAlarms, and controlMotors. Each function can be developed and tested independently. ReadSensors returns the raw measurements; updateDisplay accepts those values and handles presentation; checkAlarms evaluates thresholds and triggers alerts; controlMotors handles actuators based on computed commands. When you structure code this way, you can unit-test logic in isolation or simulate inputs without hardware. Another benefit is clearer naming: a function name conveys intent and becomes documentation. A common pitfall is over-splitting into too many tiny functions that create overhead; aim for balanced boundaries where each function is meaningful and testable. This approach also makes it easier to reuse or replace parts as a project evolves. Refactoring means extracting repeated or related code into functions. Consider a long loop that reads a sensor, prints the value, and blinks an LED. In the before state, all logic is inline: reading, formatting, printing, and blinking are mixed together. That makes it hard to change any part without touching others. In the after state, extract readSensor to return the raw reading, printValue to accept the reading and handle formatting and printing, and blinkLED to perform the blink action. Now the main loop simply calls these three functions in order. Each small function can be tested independently: simulate a reading and verify print formatting, test blink parameters without touching sensor code. Using this pattern also reduces duplication if you later need to read and print a different sensor: reuse the same printValue function.
